_meta.title: Family and Friends 5 — Grammar Reference
_meta.note: Each structure includes form, examples, common errors, and a teaching note for lesson generation.

structures.name: Present perfect with 'just'
structures.concept: An action that happened very recently

form.question: Have/Has + subject + just + past participle + ?
form.shortAnswer: Yes, I/we have. / No, I/we haven't. / Yes, he/she has. / No, he/she hasn't.

affirmative: She has just finished her homework.
negative: I haven't just woken up — I've been awake for hours.
She hasn't just started — she's nearly finished.
questions: Have you just seen that film?
Has she just left the house?

commonErrors.explanation: Past participle of 'go' is 'gone', not 'went'
Past participle of 'eat' is 'eaten', not 'ate'
'Just' goes between 'have/has' and the past participle

structures.teachingNote: Emphasise the position of 'just': it always comes between 'have/has' and the past participle. Use gestures (just now, a moment ago) to reinforce the 'very recently' meaning.
structures.vietnameseNote: Tương đương 'vừa mới' trong tiếng Việt: 'Tôi vừa mới về nhà' = 'I have just arrived home'

structures.name: Present perfect with 'ever' and 'never'
structures.concept: Talking about life experiences — things you have or have never done

form.question: Have/Has + subject + ever + past participle + ?
form.affirmativeAnswer: Yes, I/we have. / Yes, he/she has.
form.negativeAnswer: No, I/we haven't. / No, he/she hasn't.

questions: Have you ever seen a polar bear?
Has she ever been to London?
Have they ever climbed a mountain?
affirmativeAnswers: Yes, I have. I saw one at the zoo.
Yes, she has. She visited London last year.

structures.keyDistinction: 'Ever' is used in questions. 'Never' is used in negative statements (never replaces not). Do not say 'I have not never' — this is a double negative.

commonErrors.error: Have you ever been see a lion?
commonErrors.correction: Have you ever seen a lion?
commonErrors.explanation: Use only the past participle after 'ever', not 'been + infinitive'

commonErrors.error: I have never not eaten pizza.
commonErrors.explanation: Double negative — 'never' already makes the sentence negative

commonErrors.error: Has he ever go to France?
commonErrors.correction: Has he ever been to France?
commonErrors.explanation: For places, use 'been to' not 'go'

structures.teachingNote: Practise with a class survey: 'Have you ever...?' — students ask and answer in pairs, then report to class. This makes the structure feel natural and communicative.
structures.vietnameseNote: 'Have you ever...?' = 'Bạn đã từng...chưa?' | 'I have never...' = 'Tôi chưa bao giờ...'

structures.name: have to / don't have to
structures.concept: Obligation (must do) vs absence of obligation (not necessary to do)

form.obligation: Subject + have to / has to + base verb
form.noObligation: Subject + don't have to / doesn't have to + base verb
form.question: Do/Does + subject + have to + base verb + ?
form.shortAnswer: Yes, I/we do. / No, I/we don't. / Yes, he/she does. / No, he/she doesn't.

obligation: I have to vacuum the floor every day.
She has to do her homework before dinner.
They have to wear a uniform at school.
noObligation: You don't have to cook dinner — we're having takeaway.
He doesn't have to wake up early on Sundays.
They don't have to wear a uniform at weekends.
questions: Do you have to do chores at home?
Does she have to work on Saturdays?

keyDistinction.haveToVsMust: Both express obligation. 'Must' is stronger/more formal; 'have to' is more everyday. For this level, focus on 'have to'.
keyDistinction.dontHaveToVsMustnot: DON'T HAVE TO = not necessary (you can choose); MUSTN'T = prohibited (you must NOT do it). This is a common confusion point.

commonErrors.explanation: Third person singular requires 'doesn't'

commonErrors.error: I have to not wash the dishes.
commonErrors.correction: I don't have to wash the dishes.
commonErrors.explanation: Negative is 'don't/doesn't have to', not 'have to not'

structures.teachingNote: The don't have to / mustn't distinction is critical. Create clear contrast: 'You don't have to wear a helmet (but you can)' vs 'You mustn't run near the pool (it's against the rules)'.
structures.vietnameseNote: 'have to' = 'phải (làm việc gì đó)' | 'don't have to' = 'không cần phải (không bắt buộc)'

structures.name: should / shouldn't

form.question: Should + subject + base verb + ?
form.shortAnswer: Yes, you/he/she should. / No, you/he/she shouldn't.

advice: You should rest and drink lots of water.
She should see a doctor about that rash.
They should wear sunscreen at the beach.
againstAdvice: You shouldn't eat so much sugar.
He shouldn't stay up late when he has a test.
She shouldn't go to school with a fever.
questions: Should I take medicine for this headache?

commonErrors.explanation: After modal verbs (should, must, will), use the base verb WITHOUT 'to'
Modal verbs never add -s for third person singular

structures.teachingNote: Role-play is ideal for this structure. One student describes a problem; the other gives advice using should/shouldn't. Then swap. Use real-life scenarios: headache, stomachache, tired.

structures.name: Countable/uncountable nouns; some / any; how much / how many

form.countable: Things you can count individually — a banana, two apples, three eggs
form.uncountable: Things you cannot count individually — water, rice, sugar, milk
form.some: Used in affirmative sentences with both countable and uncountable
form.any: Used in questions and negative sentences
form.howMany: How many + countable noun? (How many eggs do we need?)
form.howMuch: How much + uncountable noun? (How much sugar is in this?)

some: I need some apples from the market. (countable)
There is some milk in the fridge. (uncountable)
Can I have some water, please? (polite request)
any: Are there any eggs in the fridge? (question)
howManyHowMuch: How many oranges do you want?
How much butter do I need?
How many students are in your class?

commonErrors.explanation: 'Information' is uncountable in English — no plural 's'

commonErrors.error: How many milk do we need?
commonErrors.correction: How much milk do we need?
commonErrors.explanation: 'Milk' is uncountable — use 'how much'
Use 'any' in negative sentences, not 'some'

structures.teachingNote: Play a 'What's in the fridge?' game with picture cards. Students say what they can and can't see using some/any. Then create a shopping list together.
structures.vietnameseNote: 'some' = 'một ít, một số' | 'any' = (dùng trong câu hỏi và phủ định) | 'how much/how many' = 'bao nhiêu'

structures.name: must / mustn't

form.obligation: Subject + must + base verb (strong obligation or rule)
form.prohibition: Subject + mustn't + base verb (forbidden — you must NOT do this)

obligation: You must wear a seatbelt in the car.
You must wash your hands before eating.
prohibition: You mustn't run near the swimming pool.
You mustn't touch the electric fence.
Students mustn't use phones during the exam.

keyDistinctionFromUnit3.dontHaveTo: Not necessary — but you can if you want

commonErrors.error: You must to wear a helmet.
commonErrors.explanation: No 'to' after modal verbs
Modal verbs never add -s

structures.teachingNote: Create a list of classroom/school rules. Students identify which are 'must' rules and which are 'mustn't' rules. Compare: 'You don't have to wear a tie (not compulsory) vs You mustn't wear jewellery (forbidden)'.

structures.name: will / won't for predictions and future plans

form.question: Will + subject + base verb + ?
form.shortAnswer: Yes, I/we/he/she will. / No, I/we/he/she won't.

predictions: In 50 years, robots will do most household chores.
Will people live on Mars in the future?
I think technology will make our lives easier.
She won't need to drive — her car will drive itself.
futurePlans: He won't be at school on Friday.
Will you come to my party?

structures.contraction: 'will' contracts to 'll in informal writing: 'I'll', 'she'll', 'they'll'. 'will not' contracts to 'won't' (NOT 'willn't').

commonErrors.error: I think robots will can cook.
commonErrors.correction: I think robots will be able to cook.
commonErrors.explanation: Two modals cannot be used together. Use 'be able to' after 'will'
No 'to' after 'will'
The contraction of 'will not' is 'won't', not 'willn't'

structures.teachingNote: Ask students to make 3 predictions about the world in 50 years. Then vote on which predictions the class agrees with. Use opinion starters: 'I think...', 'I believe...', 'I'm sure...'.

structures.name: Defining relative clauses with who / which / that
structures.concept: Adding essential information to identify a person, place, or thing

form.who: Used for PEOPLE — 'A teacher is a person who teaches students.'
form.which: Used for THINGS/ANIMALS — 'A violin is an instrument which has four strings.'
form.that: Can replace both who and which in defining clauses — 'A person that is kind is easy to like.'

who: She is the artist who painted the Mona Lisa.
The boy who sits next to me is very funny.
A doctor is someone who helps people when they are sick.
which: The painting which hangs in the hall is very old.
A drum is an instrument which you hit with sticks.
This is the camera which my uncle gave me.
that: The song that won the competition was amazing.
The girl that plays the violin is in my class.
This is the book that I told you about.

keyPoints: The relative clause immediately follows the noun it describes
Defining clauses give ESSENTIAL information — without them, the sentence is unclear
Do NOT use commas around defining relative clauses

commonErrors.error: She is the girl which won the prize.
commonErrors.correction: She is the girl who won the prize.
commonErrors.explanation: 'Who' for people, 'which' for things

commonErrors.error: The book which I read it was great.
commonErrors.correction: The book which I read was great.
commonErrors.explanation: Do not repeat the pronoun inside the relative clause

structures.teachingNote: Play a definitions game: one student describes something using a relative clause, others guess what it is. Example: 'It's a thing which you play music on and it has strings.' → violin
structures.vietnameseNote: Mệnh đề quan hệ xác định: 'who' cho người, 'which' cho vật | Không dùng dấu phẩy | Tương đương 'mà/mà...đó' trong tiếng Việt
